title: else and else if
description: Choosing exactly one path out of several, and why the order of the tests matters.

content.text: If it is sunny you get ice cream, otherwise fruit. You always get exactly one of the two, never both and never neither.

steps.note: The condition was false, so C++ takes the `else` path.
After the whole if/else, this always runs.

content.title: Follow the false path
content.outro: `else` has no condition of its own. It is everything the `if` did not catch.

items.title: Two conditions
items.text: Works, but you must keep two tests exact opposites.

items.title: else
items.text: One test. Between them they cover every score.

content.title: Why not two opposite ifs?
content.caption: Change one condition and forget the other, and some score falls through both. `else` cannot drift out of step.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `7 > 10` is false, so the `else` block runs.

content.title: Checked top to bottom
content.caption: The first true test wins. After that the rest of the chain is never even looked at.

steps.note: Is `80 >= 90`? No. Move down the ladder.
Run it. The chain is now finished.

content.title: Which branch wins?
content.outro: 80 is also `>= 60` and `>= 40`, but those tests never run. Separate `if`s would check them all; a chain stops at the first true one.

content.question: What does the ladder print when `marks` is `65`?
content.explain: `65 >= 90` and `65 >= 75` are false. `65 >= 60` is true, so `Grade: C` prints and the chain stops.

content.value: Because the first true test wins, the order of a chain is part of its meaning. A wrong order still compiles and runs.

content.caption: Top marks of 95 came out as a D. Every mark of 40 or more passes the first test, so nothing below it can run. Put the strictest test first.

items.title: Says too much
items.text: Works, but `&& marks < 90` is already known. Change a band and you edit two numbers.

items.title: Just enough
items.text: Anything reaching the second test is below 90 already.

content.title: Do not repeat the bound
content.caption: Read a chain aloud with "otherwise": if 90 or more, A, otherwise if 75 or more, B. If it makes sense, the order is right.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `35 > 20` is true first, so `Warm` prints and the `else if` is skipped, even though `35 > 30` is also true.

content.value: The Final else Is a Safety Net

items.sub: A rating of 0 or -3 still gets an answer instead of silence.

items.text: It lets a chain choose a value
items.sub: Declare the variable first, then assign it in every branch.

output: That is not a rating from 1 to 5.
content.caption: Without the last `else`, a rating of 0 would print nothing and the program would look broken.

steps.note: Declare `category`. A `string` with no value starts empty.
Declare `price`. An `int` with no value holds leftover garbage.
Both now have a value, so they can be printed.

content.title: A chain that picks values

content.value: C++ does not check that every path sets the variable. Swap the last `else` for `else if (age >= 13 && age < 120)` and an age of 150 prints a random garbage price. End the chain with a plain `else`, and start variables with a value, like `int price = 0;`.
content.title: C++ will not catch a missing branch

content.question: A chain sets `int price;` in every branch except one. That branch runs. What prints?
options: A garbage number that can change every run
content.explain: An `int` declared with no value holds whatever was left in memory. C++ does not stop you, so give it a starting value.

practice.question: Ask for a number and print whether it is positive, negative, or zero. Use an `if`, an `else if` and an `else`.
This gives every student a D. Reorder the chain so that 95 prints A and 65 prints C.
Ask for a month number and print the season: 12, 1 or 2 is Winter, 3 to 5 is Spring, 6 to 8 is Summer, 9 to 11 is Autumn. Add a final `else` for anything that is not 1 to 12.
Run this: the price for a 70 year old is a number the program never set. Add a final `else` that gives seniors a price of 100, then also start `price` at 0 when you declare it.

quiz.question: In an `if` and `else` pair, how many blocks run?
options: One or both, depending on the condition
quiz.explain: The `else` covers every case the `if` did not, so exactly one of the two always runs.

quiz.question: In an `else if` chain, which block runs when three conditions are all true?
options: Only the first true one, and the rest are skipped
quiz.explain: C++ tests from the top and stops at the first true condition. That is what makes a chain pick exactly one alternative.

quiz.question: Why does this chain give 95 a grade of D?  `if (marks >= 40) D else if (marks >= 90) A`
options: The loosest test comes first, so it catches every mark of 40 or more.
quiz.explain: The first true test wins, and 95 passes `>= 40`. Range tests must be ordered from narrowest to widest.

quiz.question: In a chain that already tested `marks >= 90` first, why is `marks >= 75 && marks < 90` more than you need?
options: `&&` cannot be used inside an `else if`.
Anything reaching the second test is already below 90.
It is wrong: it would miss a mark of 89.
quiz.explain: The earlier test has already removed everything at 90 or above, so the extra upper bound can only be true. One condition is fewer things to keep in step.

quiz.question: `int price;` is set inside a chain, but no branch matches. What does `cout << price;` print?
options: A garbage number left over in memory
Nothing: the program refuses to compile
quiz.explain: C++ does not check that every path sets a variable. End the chain with a plain `else`, and start variables with a value such as `int price = 0;`.
